text: Stephen Rodger Waugh AO (born 2 June 1965) is an Australian former international cricketer and twin brother of cricketer Mark Waugh. A right-handed batsman and medium-pace bowler, Waugh is considered one of the greatest cricketers of all time. He was part of the Australian team that won their first World Cup title in 1987. As captain from 1997 to 2004, he led Australia to fifteen of their record sixteen consecutive Test wins and to victory in the 1999 Cricket World Cup. Waugh is regarded as the most successful Test captain in history with 41 victories and a winning ratio of 72%. Born in New South Wales, he began his first-class cricket career in 1984 and captained the Australian Test team from 1999 to 2004, becoming the most capped Test player in history with 168 appearances until Sachin Tendulkar of India surpassed this record in 2010. He was the world number 1 all-rounder in both Test and One Day International (ODI) cricket until back issues forced him to stop bowling, after which he focused solely on batting and became one of the leading batsmen of his era. He is one of only fourteen players to have scored more than 10,000 Test runs. Waugh was named Australian of the Year in 2004 for his philanthropy and was inducted into the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in January 2010 in front of his home fans at the Sydney Cricket Ground. He has been included in the National Trust of Australia's list of one hundred Australian Living Treasures and has received the Order of Australia and the Australian Sports Medal. Known as an attacking and sometimes ruthlessly efficient captain, cricket columnist Simon Barnes described him in 2003 as a "cold-blooded, scientific" leader, noting that "Waugh wants to defeat you personally." At the end of his final Test match, he was carried by teammates in a lap of honour at the Sydney Cricket Ground. In a 2017 fan poll by the CA, he was named in the country's best Ashes XI in the last 40 years. Born at Canterbury Hospital in Campsie, South-Western Sydney, Waugh was one of twin boys born to Rodger and Beverley Waugh, arriving four minutes before Mark, who also played for Australia. Their father was a bank official and their mother a teacher in the New South Wales Department of Education. The family settled in Panania. The twins were later joined by brothers Dean (who played first-class cricket) and Danny (who played first grade for Sydney University Cricket Club). From an early age, the children were introduced to sport; by six, they were playing organised soccer, tennis, and cricket, and both were dismissed for ducks in their first match. Their paternal grandfather Edward was a greyhound trainer who played for the New South Wales Country rugby league team and was about to join Eastern Suburbs before retiring due to family reasons. Rodger was Edward's only son and was a promising junior tennis player, ranked eighth in Australia and state champion at under-14 level. On the maternal side, Bev was a tennis player who won the under-14 singles at the South Australian Championships; her eldest brother Dion Bourne was an opening batsman who played for Bankstown and remains the club's leading runscorer. The twins joined the Bankstown District under-10s at age eight and were the youngest ever selected for the New South Wales Primary Schools' soccer team in 1976. They won the Umbro International Shield, scoring all three goals in the final, and were key in their school's consecutive state cricket championships and second place in the state tennis final. In his final year, Steve was vice-captain of the cricket team and captained the state soccer team. They were instrumental in New South Wales winning the cricket carnival without a defeat, combining for a 150-run partnership in one match. As their sports demands increased, conflicts arose, and one of them was delisted from a team due to commitment issues. They attended East Hills Boys Technology High School, known for producing Australian international athletes. At 13, they were invited by their uncle Bourne, then captain of Bankstown's first grade team, to trial for the under-16 Green Shield team, and both were selected. At 14, they made their senior grade cricket debut in 1979–1980 in the Fourth XI and broke into the East Hills Boys First XI that season, achieving the same in soccer. In 1980–81, they were promoted to the Third XI mid-season. They often formed a two-man team, taking 16/85 between them. In 1980, they were selected for the state under-16 team at the national carnival. They changed soccer teams to play in the reserve grade for Sydney Croatia, earning small professional payments, but left quickly as cricket took precedence. They were promoted to Bankstown's Second XI before being selected for the First XI in the 1982–83 season at age 17, both making their debut against Western Suburbs, though Waugh was later dropped back to the Second XI. He was regarded as an aggressive player, a trait that defined his early international career. The twins finished high school in 1983. In 1983–84, both were part of New South Wales Combined High Schools and the state under-19 team; Waugh scored 170 against Great Public Schools. They were first selected for Australia in the national under-19 team to play a Test and ODI series against Sri Lanka. In the Third Test at Melbourne, Waugh scored 187 as Australia won 1–0. After high school, Waugh enrolled in a teaching course but withdrew after a few lectures. He made his maiden First XI century during the season, scoring a ton against Sydney University and Waverley. At the start of the 1984–85 season, both were included in the New South Wales state squad. At the end of the season, they signed a contract to play for Egerton Cricket Club in the Bolton League in Lancashire, with Steve officially designated as a professional but splitting earnings with Mark. They were billeted with a local family. During the year, the Australian rebel tour to South Africa occurred, breaking the apartheid boycott, leading to some players defecting; Dave Gilbert was promoted to the national squad, forfeiting his Esso scholarship, and Steve was selected to replace him with Essex, leaving Mark as the only professional. In December 2017, his son Austin Waugh was named in Australia's squad for the 2018 Under-19 Cricket World Cup. Waugh made his first-class debut for New South Wales in 1984–85, batting at number nine and bowling medium pace. In the Sheffield Shield final that season, he scored 71 while batting with the tail to help NSW win. After ten first-class matches for NSW, he made his Test debut against India in the 1985–86 season in the Second Test at Melbourne, scoring 13 and 5 and taking 2/36 in the first innings. He scored only 26 runs in four innings during the series and was retained for the tour of New Zealand, where he had a good all-round performance in the Second Test at Christchurch, scoring 74 and claiming 4/56, though his batting average remained 17.40. In the one-day format, he made his debut against New Zealand at the MCG, taking 1/13 and a catch, and did not bat as the match was washed out. He played in all 12 matches of the triangular tournament, scoring 266 runs at 38.00 with two half-centuries, including a top score of 81 in the Australia Day victory over India, and took seven wickets at 33.00. He played in all four ODIs on the tour of New Zealand, scoring 111 runs at 27.75 and taking four wickets at 39.75. The Australian selectors retained him for a tour of India in 1986, despite scoring only 113 runs at 12.56 in his Test career. In the three Tests, he scored 59 runs once and took two wickets. As a bowler, he bore a heavy workload, though selected primarily for his batting. He played in all six ODIs, scoring 111 runs at 55.50 and taking seven wickets at 35.86. In the First Test against England at Brisbane in 1986–87, he bowled a long spell, taking 3/76, then scored 0 and 28 as Australia lost. In the Second Test at Perth, he made 71 and had match figures of 5/159, including 5/69 in the second innings, and scored 79 not out in the drawn Third Test at Adelaide. His scores of 49 and 73 in the last two Tests gave him series figures of 310 runs (at 44.29) and ten wickets (at 33.60), a fighting effort in a team defeated 1–2. The win in the Fifth Test was the first time Waugh was in a victorious Test team in his 13th match. He played in all 13 ODIs for the home season, scoring 372 runs at 37.20 with two half-centuries and taking 21 wickets at 21.80. He regularly performed with both bat and ball; against Pakistan, he scored 82 and took 4/48 but could not stop a one-wicket victory, then scored 83* and took 2/30 in an Australia Day win over England. He failed to maintain form in the finals, scoring one and one and taking 1/78 as England won 2–0. Early in his career, Waugh was a natural, uninhibited strokeplayer who liked to drive off the back foot, scoring quickly but inconsistently at Test level and was better suited to ODI cricket. As a bowler, he was known for his astute change of pace and was the pioneer in inventing a carefully disguised slower ball bowled from the back of the hand, regularly used in the final overs, where his change of pace was difficult to score from. Allan Border often used Waugh as a final overs specialist in crucial situations, and at his peak, he was the top slog overs specialist bowler for any conditions. The 1987 World Cup, played on the Indian subcontinent, marked a turning point in Waugh's career. He scored 19* in the death overs against India in the first match, and his tight bowling in the closing overs ended with the dismissal of Maninder Singh in the final over, securing a one-run victory. In the match against Zimbabwe, he scored 45 and conceded only seven runs in six overs, leading to a 96-run win. Against New Zealand, he bowled the last over when the Kiwis needed seven runs, restricting them to three runs by taking two wickets, ending with 2/36. In the second round robin, he took 1/59 and scored 42 in a 56-run loss to India, then took 2/37 in a 17-run win over New Zealand. In Australia's final group match, he scored 10* and took 1/9 from four overs in a 70-run win over Zimbabwe. Australia qualified for the semi-finals and faced co-hosts Pakistan in Lahore. Batting first, Waugh hit 16 from the final over of the innings in a cameo of 32*, helping Australia win by 18 runs. In the final, he scored an unbeaten five in a brief innings at the end of the innings. He was a key player as Australia defended a target of 254 against England at Kolkata, claiming the wickets of Allan Lamb and Phillip DeFreitas in the 47th and 49th overs as England faltered. Australia won by seven runs to claim the World Cup for the first time. Waugh compiled 167 runs at 55.66 and took 11 wickets at 26.18. These performances in tight situations earned him the nickname "Iceman." However, he remained inconsistent in Test matches, scoring only 194 runs at 32.33 in five Tests in 1987–88 against New Zealand, England, and Sri Lanka, with nine wickets at 29.67. His ODI form remained strong, playing in all 11 ODIs, scoring 226 runs at 32.29 and taking 18 wickets at 23.50, including a 4/33 in a match against Sri Lanka. In a Test tour of Pakistan in late 1988, he scored 92 runs at 18.40 with one half-century and two wickets at 108.00. In 1988–89 against the West Indies, he mixed batting failures with two entertaining innings of 90 and 91 on the faster pitches of Brisbane and Perth. He bowled bouncers at Viv Richards at Brisbane, claiming 3/77 and 5/92 in the Third Test at Melbourne. Bill O'Reilly wrote that the most significant incident of the Brisbane Test was the three consecutive bouncers Waugh served up to Viv Richards, which he described as an uncompromising message to the West Indies captain about the end of the bouncer policy. Waugh continued to perform well in ODIs, scoring 270 runs at 38.57 and taking seven wickets at 49.42, with his highest score and best bowling analysis occurring in the same match—taking 3/57 before scoring 54 against the West Indies in Melbourne. Despite this, Australia lost the match. Heading into the 1989 Ashes series, Waugh's batting average was 30.52 from 26 Tests. In the three-match ODI series before the Tests, he scored 113 runs at 37.66 and took three wickets at 54.00. Waugh finally scored his maiden Test century, 177 not out in the First Test at Leeds, a free-flowing innings marked by square driving that lasted just over five hours and helped Australia set a strong platform for a win. Waugh scored 270 runs at 38.57 and took seven wickets at 49.42, with his highest score and best bowling analysis occurring in the same match—taking 3/57 before scoring 54 against West Indies in Melbourne—despite Australia losing the game. Heading into the 1989 Ashes series, his batting average was 30.52 from 26 Tests; in the preceding three-match ODI series, he scored 113 runs at 37.66 and took three wickets at 54.00. He scored his maiden Test century, 177 not out, in the First Test at Leeds, a free-flowing innings marked by square driving that lasted over five hours and helped Australia set a large first-innings total. He followed with an unbeaten 152 in the Second Test at Lord's, guiding his tail partners to build a 242-run first-innings lead, and was not dismissed until the first innings of the Third Test for 43, by which time he had 393 runs. He scored 92 in the Fourth Test at Old Trafford in a win and did not pass 20 in the last two Tests, finishing the series with 506 runs at 126.5; he bowled only twice, taking two wickets, and first experienced back problems that would hinder his bowling. On the brief India Nehru Cup ODI tour after the Ashes, he played as a specialist batsman, scoring 88 runs at 22.00 and not bowling. During the 1989/90 international season, he scored 378 runs at 37.8 in six Tests in Australia and one in New Zealand; the highlight was an unbeaten 134 against Sri Lanka in the Second Test in Hobart, following twin half-centuries in the First Test. His focus on batting resulted in only 1/19 with the ball in seven Tests. His Test form tapered off thereafter. In ODIs, Australia played ten at home and five in New Zealand; after taking two wickets at 38.50 in the first three ODIs, Waugh did not bowl again. After scoring only 99 runs at 19.80 in the first nine ODIs in Australia, he was dropped for the Second Final against Pakistan, which Australia won. He played in all five ODIs in New Zealand, scoring only 72 runs at 18.00. He returned to bowling in the Sharjah tournament, taking four wickets at 28.00 and scoring 98 runs at 49.00. In 1990, Waugh and his twin brother Mark scored an unbeaten 464 in 407 minutes for NSW against Western Australia at the WACA Ground, setting a world first-class record; both teams were at full strength and WA's attack included Test bowlers Terry Alderman, Bruce Reid, and Chris Matthews, with the twins ending on 216 and 229 respectively. During the 1990–91 Ashes series in Australia, Waugh suffered a form slump, making only 82 runs at 20.50, and was dropped for the Fourth Test at Adelaide; he was replaced by his twin Mark, who scored a century on debut. However, he remained a regular in the ODI team, playing in all ten ODIs, scoring 141 runs at 35.25 and taking seven wickets at 49.42. Recalled for the Third Test in Trinidad during the 1991 Caribbean tour, he and Mark became the first twins to play in a Test match together; however, he failed to post a significant score and was dropped for the Fifth Test, Australia's only win in the series. He played in all five ODIs, scoring 86 runs at 28.66 and taking five wickets at 30.60. Waugh remained out of the Test team for eighteen months and did not play in the five-day format during the 1991–92 season. Nevertheless, he played in all 18 ODIs, scoring only 146 runs at 18.25 but consistently taking 16 wickets at 19.00. As a result, he retained his position in the team for all eight of Australia's group matches in the 1992 Cricket World Cup in Australia and New Zealand, scoring 187 runs at 26.71 and taking eight wickets at 34.63; he scored 55 and took 2/28 in a 128-run win over Zimbabwe as Australia failed to progress beyond the group stage. He returned as number three batsman for the 1992–93 home Test series against the West Indies, with a 228-run average at 25.33 bolstered by a 100 in the Third Test in Sydney; Waugh called this "probably the most important hundred of my Test career ... word had reached me that if I didn't get runs, then I was going to be dropped." He continued to be a fixture in the ODI team, playing in all ten matches and scoring 213 runs at 23.66 with one half-century and taking nine wickets at 39.22. Solid performances in New Zealand, where he scored 178 Test runs at 44.50, enabled him to hold his position on the 1993 Ashes tour of England. He completed the tour with 120 runs at 30.00 and three wickets at 57.66 in five ODIs; the three-match ODI series in England preceded the Tests and Waugh scored 41 runs at 20.50 and took five wickets at 30.20. During the Test series, Michael Slater became the regular opener and Boon returned to the middle order; Waugh gained the number six position ahead of two promising Western Australians, Justin Langer and Damien Martyn. In the Fourth Test at Headingley, Waugh's 157 not out earned comparisons to his 1989 efforts and he shared an unbroken stand of 332 with Allan Border. He also scored half-centuries in the First and Fifth Tests and ended with 416 at 83.2 from limited opportunities—playing nine innings, only five of which were completed. Australia's top order dominated the English attack, and the tourists retained the Ashes 4–1. Returning to Australia, he solidified his position by scoring an unbeaten 147 against New Zealand in an innings victory in the Third Test at Brisbane, ending the series with 216 runs once dismissed. He missed part of the 1993–94 triangular ODI tournament with New Zealand and South Africa due to a hamstring injury in late December, as well as the first two Tests against the South Africans. He returned for the end of the ODIs and ended with 141 runs at 23.50 and taking four wickets at 54.50. Waugh played in the Third Test at Adelaide Oval in late January with Australia trailing 1–0; he scored a 160 and took 4/26 as Australia won the Test and levelled the series. He was named international player of the [Australian] season. He took 5/28 and scored 86 in the Second Test of the return series in South Africa at Newlands, Cape Town, helping Australia level the series 1–1 after losing the first at Wanderers in Johannesburg. Another half-century saw him end with 195 runs at 65.00 and his bowling was at its most productive in five years, with 10 wickets at 13.00. In the ODI series, he received the player of the series for his all-round efforts, which hauled Australia back from a deficit of 2–4 to draw the series at 4–4; he took 2/48 in the final match as Australia levelled the series by one run, ending with 291 runs at 48.50 and five wickets at 56.40. At the conclusion of the tour, the Australian Cricket Board interviewed Waugh, along with David Boon, Mark Taylor, and Ian Healy to determine their opinions on the team's direction after Allan Border's impending retirement; despite Waugh's greater experience, Taylor was granted the captaincy and Healy was made vice-captain. The new leadership took the team to Sri Lanka for the Singer World Series ODI tournament and then on a Test-playing tour of Pakistan; Waugh scored 53 runs at 17.66 and took five wickets in 16.20. On the latter tour, he made 73 in the First Test, which Australia lost by one wicket; his 98 in the Second Test at Rawalpindi was notable for his survival against a hostile barrage of short-pitched bowling from Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, falling when a bouncer struck his body and rolled onto the stumps. A shoulder injury forced him out of the final Test, which Australia drew and therefore lost the series. Waugh scored 153 runs at 38.25 with two half-centuries and took two wickets at 72.00 as Australia won the ODI tournament. During the 1994–95 Ashes series against England, he narrowly missed centuries in the Second and Fifth Test in Melbourne and Perth, scoring 94 and 99 not out respectively when the last wicket fell; in the second instance, his brother Mark was run out after a mix-up while running for the injured Craig McDermott. It was an uneven series performance, scoring 94* and 26* in the Second Test and 99* and 80 in the Fifth, but not passing 20 in the six innings of the other three Tests; he ended the series with 345 at 49.28 and did not bowl for the entire series. Waugh played only one ODI for the season, scoring a duck and not bowling a ball. The season ended with a short ODI tournament in New Zealand, which Australia won; Waugh scored 81 runs at 27.00 in four matches and did not bowl. The West Indies had been Australia's bête noire since winning the Frank Worrell Trophy in 1978; at the beginning of Australia's 1995 tour of the Caribbean, the West Indies had not lost a Test series since 1980 and had not lost a Test series to Australia at home since 1973. The Tests were preceded by an ODI series lost 1–4; Waugh scored 164 runs at 32.80 and took three wickets at 41.00. In a low-scoring, four-Test series, Waugh compiled 429 runs at an average of 107.25 and claimed five wickets (for 62 runs), winning the player of the series award; his twin Mark was the next best batsman with 240 runs at 40.00. During the First Test at Barbados, Waugh claimed a low catch from Brian Lara in the first innings; television replays were inconclusive but suggested the ball may have hit the ground; Lara, known for accepting the word of the fielder without question, left the field. Following his dismissal, the West Indies' batting collapsed, and Australia won by ten wickets. Waugh later faced accusations of dishonesty and cheating over the incident. After scoring 65 not out in the drawn Second Test at Antigua, Waugh defied the Caribbean pacemen on a green pitch at Trinidad suited to their hostile bowling during the Third Test. In the first innings, he scored an unbeaten 63 of Australia's 128 and had a mid-pitch confrontation with Curtly Ambrose; after evading a bouncer from Ambrose, the pair exchanged glares, Waugh swore and told Ambrose to return to his bowling mark; an angry Ambrose had to be physically dragged away by his captain—a photograph of this moment became one of the iconic images of cricket in the 1990s, symbolising when Australia was no longer intimidated by the West Indies. Waugh "showed he was prepared to put it all on the line," said Justin Langer, "in the toughest conditions [...] against probably the best fast bowler of our time. To stand up to him [Ambrose] and go toe to toe [...] gave us a huge boost." Nevertheless, the West Indies won the match and levelled the series. In the decider in Jamaica, Waugh took 2/14 in the West Indies' first innings of 265 and then arrived at the crease with Australia at 73 for three in reply; he compiled a long partnership of 231 runs with his brother Mark, who was eventually out for 126; Waugh was the last man to go, out for 200 after nine hours of batting. "Steve had made up his mind to bat and bat," wrote Paul Reiffel, "to stay out there and anchor the proceedings. [... H]e copped a lot of blows on his arms, chest and ribs. When he came back to the dressing room at the end of day two, we could see the spots and bruises on his body [...]. I remember when I walked in [...] he didn't say anything to me, but then he didn't need to. We all pretty much knew that we just had to support him." He was in a trance-like state; in the wee hours of the second morning, a security guard was found rifling through Steve's kit bag. That incident did not affect his concentration. It all just went to show how strong a character he was. Waugh played patiently and reached his double century with an all-run four to fine-leg off a quicker ball from Carl Hooper; he was the last man out. With a large lead on first innings, Australia dismissed the opposition for a low score to win a crushing victory. After some post-win wassailing, Waugh retired to bed in his cricket whites, socks, and baggy green. "[Y]ou could say that Steve's legacy gained a lot of momentum from his efforts at Jamaica," wrote Reiffel. Waugh started the 1995–96 Australian season ranked as the world's leading Test batsman. He made an unbeaten 112 as Australia defeated Pakistan in the First Test at Brisbane and scored 200 runs at 50.00 for the series. Suffering an injury in December, he missed the First Test against Sri Lanka and part of the triangular ODI tournament, then returned for the Boxing Day Test at Melbourne to score 131 not out. Waugh returned during the latter stages of the triangular tournament, playing in the last four matches after missing the first six. He scored his maiden ODI century, ten years after his ODI debut, with an unbeaten 102 against Sri Lanka in Melbourne. Despite this, Australia lost by three wickets. Waugh ended with 128 runs at 42.66 and did not take a wicket, bowling only four overs on his comeback from injury. He helped Australia to a 3–0 result in the Test series by scoring 170 and 61 not out at Adelaide to end the series with 362 runs for once out. He also took 4/34 in the Third Test. During the 1996 Cricket World Cup on the subcontinent, Waugh scored 82 and featured in a 207-run partnership with his brother during Australia's first match against Kenya—an Australian record partnership at the World Cup. He made an unbeaten half-century in the quarter-final against New Zealand at Madras, sealing a successful run chase. However, he was less effective in the semi-final and final, failing to pass 20 on either occasion. Australia lost the final to Sri Lanka at Lahore. After the World Cup, Geoff Marsh replaced Bob Simpson as coach. The Australians started the new era with two ODI tournaments in Sri Lanka and India. Waugh scored 366 runs at 40.66 with three half-centuries and took five wickets at 37.40 across nine matches. The tour ended with a solitary Test against India in Delhi, where Waugh was the only Australian to make a half-century in a defeat. Waugh failed to make a century in the five Tests of the 1996–97 Australian season against the West Indies, scoring 255 runs at 36.42 with three half-centuries.
